position: attributive only — *a one-time fee*, never *the fee is one-time*
contrast: For 'former', American writing usually drops the hyphen: *a onetime champion*. For 'happening once', keep it: *a one-time payment*.

senses.gloss: Happening only once, not repeated.
examples: The gym charges a *one-time* signup fee of fifty dollars.
This is a *one-time* offer, so don't wait.
Congress approved a *one-time* payment to every household.

senses.gloss: Former; in that job or role before.
examples: The *one-time* mayor now runs a bakery downtown.
Her *one-time* partner testified against her.

ru: индивидуальный, один на один; взаимно однозначный
contrast: Americans also say *one-on-one* for the teaching and meeting sense: *a one-on-one meeting*. *One-to-one* is the usual form for matching numbers.

senses.gloss: Between two people only, with no one else involved.
examples: Every student gets an hour of *one-to-one* tutoring a week.
He asked for a *one-to-one* meeting with the director.
The coaching is *one-to-one*, not in groups.

senses.gloss: Matching one item to exactly one other item.
examples: There is a *one-to-one* match between the codes and the files.
The translation is not *one-to-one*, since one Russian word can cover three English ones.

form: compound — *one* + *woman*; the noun stays singular: *a one-woman show*
contrast: *A one-woman band* keeps the singular *woman*, never *women*. The male form is *one-man*.

senses.gloss: Done or performed by a single woman.
examples: She took her *one-woman* show to three cities.
The bakery is basically a *one-woman* operation.
It was a *one-woman* campaign against the new highway.

senses.gloss: Needing a lot of effort and feeling like a burden.
examples: The new paperwork is *onerous* for small businesses.
He called the contract terms *onerous* and walked away.
Filing by hand is *more onerous* than doing it online.

contrast: Solid *onetime* means 'former'. Hyphenated *one-time* usually means 'happening once': *a one-time fee*.

senses.gloss: Former; holding that job or role at an earlier time.
examples: A *onetime* teacher, she now writes cookbooks.
The *onetime* rivals ended up starting a company together.
He interviewed his *onetime* boss for the podcast.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an ongoing investigation*; after a verb: *the search is ongoing*

senses.gloss: Still happening and not finished yet.
examples: Police would not comment on the *ongoing* investigation.
We have an *ongoing* problem with the heating.
Repairs to the bridge are *ongoing*.

position: both — *an online class*; *the store is online now*
contrast: *Online* is also an adverb: *I bought it online*. Only the use before a noun or after *be* is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Done on the internet, or connected to it.
examples: She teaches an *online* class on Tuesday nights.
Our *online* orders doubled last year.
The system will be *online* again by noon.

position: attributive only — always after *the*, *my*, *his* and the like: *the only way*
form: -ly, but an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: The adverb *only* ('just') is far more common: *I only wanted to help*. An *only child* has no brothers or sisters.

senses.gloss: Being the single one of its kind; there are no others.
examples: That's the *only* way to get there before dark.
She was the *only* person who said anything.
He's an *only* child, so the house was quiet.

senses.gloss: Sounding like the noise it names.
examples: *Buzz* and *hiss* are *onomatopoeic* words.
The poem leans on *onomatopoeic* effects.
*Splash* is *onomatopoeic* in English and in Russian.

position: both — *onshore drilling*; *the wind was onshore all day*

senses.gloss: On land rather than at sea.
examples: The company moved its *onshore* rigs to Texas.
*Onshore* wind farms are cheaper to build than sea ones.
Most of the crew live in *onshore* housing.

senses.gloss: Blowing from the sea toward the land.
examples: An *onshore* breeze kept the beach cool.
The wind turned *onshore* in the afternoon.

position: both — *her onstage persona*; *the band was onstage by nine*
contrast: *Onstage* is also an adverb, the more common use: *She walked onstage*.

senses.gloss: Happening on the stage, in front of the audience.
examples: His *onstage* persona is nothing like the man backstage.
The *onstage* banter between songs was the best part.
The opening act was *onstage* for forty minutes.

contrast: *Opaque* lets no light through at all; *translucent* lets some through, like frosted glass.

senses.gloss: Not letting light through, so you cannot see through it.
examples: The bathroom window is *opaque* for privacy.
She poured the paint into an *opaque* plastic bottle.
These tights are *more opaque* than the pair I ruined.

senses.gloss: Very hard to understand.
examples: The tax rules are *opaque* even to accountants.
His answer was deliberately *opaque*.

position: both — *an open door*; *the door is open*
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* — *open to the public*, *open to trying new things*
contrast: The state is *open*: *the door is open*. *Opened* names the action that just happened: *she opened the door*, *a newly opened store*.

senses.gloss: Not closed, shut or locked.
examples: Leave the window *open* — it's hot in here.
He ran in through the *open* gate.
Her book lay *open* on the table.

senses.gloss: Doing business, or letting people in.
examples: The pharmacy is *open* until nine.
The garden is *open* to the public on weekends.

senses.gloss: Honest and willing to talk or to listen.
examples: She's very *open* about her mistakes.
I'm *open* to suggestions if you have a better plan.
He became *more open* after a few months of therapy.

senses.gloss: Not yet decided or filled.
examples: The question of who pays is still *open*.
There are two *open* positions on the team.

ru: под открытым небом, на свежем воздухе
position: attributive only — *an open-air market*, never *the market is open-air*

senses.gloss: Outdoors, with no roof or walls.
examples: We bought peaches at the *open-air* market.
The town has an *open-air* concert every July.
They ate at an *open-air* restaurant by the water.

position: attributive only — almost always in *an open-and-shut case*

senses.gloss: So clear that there is nothing to argue about.
examples: The prosecutor called it an *open-and-shut* case.
It looked like an *open-and-shut* matter until the video turned up.
Insurance treated the claim as *open-and-shut* fraud.

ru: открытый, без чётких границ; свободный (о вопросе)

senses.gloss: With no fixed end, limit or date.
examples: They gave him an *open-ended* contract.
The strike is *open-ended*, with no return date set.
Her invitation was *open-ended* — come any weekend.

senses.gloss: Allowing any kind of answer, not just yes or no.
examples: Ask *open-ended* questions and let the child talk.
The survey ends with two *open-ended* questions.

position: both — *an open-source library*; *the whole project is open-source*

senses.gloss: Published with its source code free for anyone to read, use and change.
examples: The team built the site on *open-source* software.
He maintains two *open-source* libraries in his free time.
The whole database is *open-source* and free.

position: both — usually with an adverb in front: *a newly opened wing*; *the museum is newly opened*
contrast: A Russian speaker's classic slip: the state is *open* (*the store is open*), not *opened*. *Opened* points at the act of opening: *an opened envelope*, *a recently opened branch*.

senses.gloss: Already opened by someone, no longer sealed.
examples: An *opened* package of crackers sat on the counter.
Return the *opened* bottle to the fridge.
The mail came back with three *opened* envelopes.

senses.gloss: Started doing business a short time ago.
examples: We tried the newly *opened* Thai place on Main Street.
The recently *opened* wing holds the modern collection.

contrast: *An opening* is also a common noun — a gap, or a job that needs filling: *We have an opening in sales*.

senses.gloss: Coming first, at the start of something.
examples: The *opening* scene takes place on a train.
Her *opening* remarks lasted two minutes.
They lost their *opening* game of the season.

senses.gloss: Having to do with opera.
examples: He trained for years as an *operatic* tenor.
The festival mixes *operatic* and folk music.
Her voice is fully *operatic* in the last act.

senses.gloss: So big and dramatic that it feels staged.
examples: The breakup was *operatic*, with shouting in the street.
He has an *operatic* way of describing small problems.

senses.gloss: Having to do with running a business or a machine day to day.
examples: *Operating* costs went up again this quarter.
The plant is running below its normal *operating* capacity.
Windows and macOS are *operating* systems.

senses.gloss: Used for surgery.
examples: She was wheeled into the *operating* room at six.
The hospital added two *operating* tables.

position: both — *operational costs*; *the plant is fully operational*

senses.gloss: Working and ready to be used.
examples: The new terminal will be *operational* in March.
Only one elevator is *operational* today.
The radar was fully *operational* within a week.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the day-to-day running of something.
examples: The report lists *operational* problems at three warehouses.
She handles *operational* decisions; he handles the money.

position: both — *the operative word*; *the rule is still operative*
contrast: *An operative* is also a noun — an agent or a worker: *a CIA operative*.

senses.gloss: Being the word or part that really matters.
examples: He said he'd try — and *try* is the *operative* word.
*Cheap* was the *operative* word in that description.
The *operative* phrase here is 'up to', not 'at least'.

senses.gloss: In force and working.
examples: The old rule is no longer *operative*.
That agreement became *operative* in January.

contrast: It is usually a mild criticism — the person holds strong views and won't hear others. Not the same as *well-informed*.

senses.gloss: Holding strong opinions and saying them, often without listening.
examples: My uncle is loud and *opinionated* about everything.
It's an *opinionated* book, and that's why people read it.
She gets *more opinionated* after her second cup of coffee.

position: attributive only — almost always with *moment*, *time* or *arrival*
contrast: *Opportune* is about good timing; *opportunistic* is about using a chance, often selfishly.

senses.gloss: Coming at exactly the right time.
examples: He waited for an *opportune* moment to ask for a raise.
Your call came at an *opportune* time.
There is no *more opportune* moment than right now.

contrast: *Opportune* praises the timing; *opportunistic* usually criticizes the person for grabbing a chance without principles.

senses.gloss: Taking any chance to get an advantage, without worrying about principles.
examples: Critics called the announcement *opportunistic* and cynical.
He's an *opportunistic* investor who buys after every crash.
The goal was *opportunistic* — the keeper had slipped.

senses.gloss: Attacking a body that is already weak, about an infection.
examples: Patients on these drugs face *opportunistic* infections.
The fungus is *opportunistic* and harmless to healthy people.

position: attributive only — almost always in *opposable thumbs*

senses.gloss: Able to be placed against the other fingers, about a thumb.
examples: Humans and apes have *opposable* thumbs.
*Opposable* thumbs are what let us hold a pen.
The lesson explained why an *opposable* thumb matters for tools.

senses.gloss: On the other side in a game, a fight or a court case.
examples: The *opposing* team scored twice in the first half.
*Opposing* counsel objected before he finished the sentence.
Soldiers from the *opposing* army crossed the river at dawn.

senses.gloss: Going in the other direction; in conflict with each other.
examples: The paper prints *opposing* views on the same page.
Two *opposing* currents meet near the point.

position: both — before a noun: *the opposite side*; also after the noun: *the house opposite*
takes: *to* or *from* + noun — *the opposite to what I expected*
contrast: *Opposite* is also a noun (*the opposite is true*) and a preposition (*she sat opposite me*). Russian *напротив* covers all three.

senses.gloss: As different as possible from something else.
examples: The two brothers went in *opposite* directions.
That had the *opposite* effect from the one we wanted.
My conclusion was the *opposite* of his.

senses.gloss: Facing, on the other side.
examples: They live on the *opposite* side of the street.
The man in the seat *opposite* fell asleep.

senses.gloss: Treated cruelly and unfairly by people with power.
examples: The novel follows an *oppressed* family in the 1930s.
They fled a country where minorities were *oppressed*.
Workers in the mills felt *oppressed* by the new rules.

senses.gloss: Cruel and unfair to the people under it.
examples: They grew up under an *oppressive* government.
The rules were *oppressive* and impossible to follow.
Each new law was *more oppressive* than the last.

senses.gloss: So heavy or hot that it is hard to bear.
examples: The heat in August is *oppressive*.
An *oppressive* silence filled the room.

senses.gloss: Having to do with light or with seeing.
examples: The floor looks tilted, but it's an *optical* illusion.
The town is wired with *optical* fiber.
He polishes *optical* lenses for telescopes.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *optimal conditions*
contrast: *Optimal* already means 'the best possible', so *more optimal* sounds wrong to careful readers — say *better*.

senses.gloss: Best possible in the circumstances.
examples: Store the seeds at the *optimal* temperature of 40 degrees.
These are not *optimal* conditions for a launch.
The software finds the *optimal* route in a second.

senses.gloss: Expecting good things to happen.
examples: She's *optimistic* about her chances in the final.
He gave an *optimistic* forecast for the spring.
I'm *more optimistic* than I was a month ago.

contrast: *Optimum* is also a noun: *well below the optimum*. Before a noun, *optimal* is the more common of the two today.

senses.gloss: Giving the best result possible.
examples: June is the *optimum* time to plant them.
The engine runs at *optimum* efficiency around 2,000 rpm.
We never found the *optimum* balance between speed and cost.

position: both — *an optional course*; *the essay is optional*

senses.gloss: Up to you; you may do it or not.
examples: The second essay is *optional*.
Heated seats are an *optional* extra.
Ties are *optional* at the dinner.

senses.gloss: Rich-looking and expensive, often to the point of showing off.
examples: The hotel lobby is *opulent*, with marble everywhere.
She wore an *opulent* gold dress to the opening.
The second house was even *more opulent* than the first.

position: both — *an oral exam*; *the test is oral*
contrast: *Oral* and *aural* sound alike in American English, but *aural* is about hearing: *an aural test*.

senses.gloss: Spoken rather than written.
examples: The *oral* exam lasts fifteen minutes.
These stories come from an *oral* tradition.
Half of the grade is *oral*.

senses.gloss: Of the mouth, or taken through the mouth.
examples: Good *oral* hygiene prevents most of this.
The medicine comes in an *oral* form now.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the path of something going around a planet or star.
examples: The satellite reached its *orbital* height in an hour.
They corrected the capsule's *orbital* path twice.
*Orbital* debris is a growing problem.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *orchestral music*

senses.gloss: Written for or played by an orchestra.
examples: The concert opens with an *orchestral* suite.
He writes *orchestral* arrangements of pop songs.
The last track is purely *orchestral*.

position: both — usually with an adverb: *a carefully orchestrated campaign*

senses.gloss: Planned in careful detail, often secretly.
examples: The protest was carefully *orchestrated* down to the signs.
It looked spontaneous, but the whole evening was *orchestrated*.
Investigators found an *orchestrated* campaign of fake reviews.

senses.gloss: Arranged so an orchestra can play it.
examples: The song was *orchestrated* for strings and horns.
His richly *orchestrated* score won an award.

position: both — *an ordained minister*; *she was ordained last spring*

senses.gloss: Officially made a priest, minister or rabbi.
examples: An *ordained* minister performed the ceremony.
He is *ordained*, but he works as a carpenter.
She became an *ordained* rabbi at thirty.

position: both — *an ordinary day*; *the food was ordinary*
contrast: *Out of the ordinary* means 'unusual': *Nothing out of the ordinary happened*.

senses.gloss: Normal and not special in any way.
examples: It started as an *ordinary* Tuesday.
*Ordinary* people can't afford these rents.
The house looked *more ordinary* than in the pictures.

senses.gloss: Not very good; plain.
examples: The service was great, but the food was *ordinary*.
He gave a perfectly *ordinary* performance.

position: both — *organic milk*; *all the produce here is organic*

senses.gloss: Grown without artificial chemicals or fertilizers.
examples: She buys *organic* milk for the kids.
The farm went *organic* five years ago.
*Organic* apples cost twice as much here.

senses.gloss: Of living things, or of the chemistry of carbon compounds.
examples: *Organic* matter in the soil holds water better.
He failed *organic* chemistry the first time.

senses.gloss: Developing naturally, not forced or planned.
examples: The band's growth was *organic* — no marketing at all.
The two scenes have an *organic* connection.

contrast: American spelling has *z*: *organizational*. British writing has *organisational*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with how a company or group is run and arranged.
examples: The merger brought big *organizational* changes.
She has real *organizational* skills.
The chart shows the *organizational* structure of the agency.

position: both — *an organized person*; *she is very organized*
contrast: American spelling is *organized*; British writing has *organised*.

senses.gloss: Good at planning and keeping things in order.
examples: He's the *organized* one — he keeps all the receipts.
Try to be *more organized* about your mornings.
You need to be *organized* to run a kitchen.

senses.gloss: Arranged and run by a group, not happening on its own.
examples: The city has a real problem with *organized* crime.
*Organized* labor backed the bill.

contrast: In American English *Oriental* is offensive when used of people — say *Asian*. It is still normal for rugs, art and some plants: *an Oriental rug*.

senses.gloss: From or in the style of East Asia, now used mainly of objects.
examples: An *Oriental* rug covered most of the floor.
The museum's *Oriental* collection came from one donor.
*Oriental* poppies bloom in early June.

position: both — *a service-oriented company*; *the course is oriented toward beginners*
form: -ed from the verb *orient*; often the second half of a compound — *family-oriented*, *detail-oriented*
contrast: Americans say *oriented*; *orientated* is British and sounds odd here.

senses.gloss: Aimed at a particular group, goal or way of working.
examples: The program is *oriented* toward first-time buyers.
They want someone detail-*oriented* for this job.
Their whole business is *oriented* around repeat customers.

position: both — *the original plan*; *her work is very original*
contrast: The 'first' sense is not gradable — *the original owner*, never *more original owner*. Only the 'new and creative' sense compares.

senses.gloss: First, earliest; existing from the beginning.
examples: The *original* plan was to leave on Friday.
The house still has its *original* windows.
Who was the *original* owner of the painting?

senses.gloss: New and creative, not copied from anyone.
examples: Her thesis is genuinely *original*.
It's a funny movie, but nothing about it is *original*.
His second album is *more original* than his first.

position: both — *ornamental grasses*; *the handle is purely ornamental*

senses.gloss: There to look pretty rather than to be useful.
examples: She planted *ornamental* grasses along the fence.
The iron railing is *ornamental*, not structural.
The shop sells *ornamental* tiles from Portugal.

senses.gloss: Covered with a lot of decoration.
examples: The church has an *ornate* ceiling painted in gold.
He handed me an *ornate* silver key.
The frame is far *more ornate* than the painting inside it.

senses.gloss: Full of long words and decoration, about writing.
examples: His prose is *ornate* and hard to follow.
She cut the *ornate* opening paragraph entirely.

contrast: *Ornery* is American and informal, and it is half affectionate — often said about an old relative, a mule or a stubborn machine.

senses.gloss: Bad-tempered and hard to deal with.
examples: Grandpa gets *ornery* when he misses his nap.
That *ornery* old mule won't move for anyone.
He's *ornerier* every year, but we love him.

position: both — *orphaned children*; *she was orphaned at nine*

senses.gloss: Left with no living parents.
examples: The charity places *orphaned* children with relatives.
He was *orphaned* by the flood.
They raised two *orphaned* cousins.

senses.gloss: Left without anyone to look after it.
examples: The library digitized thousands of *orphaned* works.
Nobody wanted the *orphaned* project after the layoffs.

senses.gloss: Having to do with straightening teeth.
examples: Our plan covers half of any *orthodontic* work.
She needs *orthodontic* treatment before the surgery.
The clinic sells *orthodontic* wax for sore spots.

position: both — *orthodox methods*; *his views are not orthodox*
contrast: Capitalized, *Orthodox* names a branch of a religion: *the Russian Orthodox Church*, *Orthodox Judaism*.

senses.gloss: Following the usual, accepted ideas or methods.
examples: The treatment is *orthodox* and well tested.
His coaching style is anything but *orthodox*.
She takes a *more orthodox* view of the evidence.

senses.gloss: Strictly following the traditional rules of a religion.
examples: They keep an *orthodox* kitchen with separate dishes.
He grew up in an *orthodox* family in Brooklyn.

contrast: American spelling is *orthopedic*; British writing has *orthopaedic*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with bones, joints and muscles and how they are treated.
examples: He sees an *orthopedic* surgeon about his knee.
The store sells *orthopedic* shoes.
She bought an *orthopedic* mattress for her back.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *Orwellian surveillance*

senses.gloss: Like the frightening state in Orwell's novels: watching everyone and twisting the truth.
examples: Critics called the tracking law *Orwellian*.
Cameras on every corner give the place an *Orwellian* feel.
Renaming the layoffs 'a talent refresh' was pure *Orwellian* language.

senses.gloss: Moving or swinging back and forth again and again.
examples: An *oscillating* fan kept the room bearable.
The tool uses an *oscillating* blade for tight corners.
He measured the *oscillating* current across the coil.

contrast: *Ostensible* signals doubt: the stated reason is probably not the real one. The adverb *ostensibly* is far more common in speech.

senses.gloss: Given as the reason or purpose, though probably not the true one.
examples: The *ostensible* reason for the trip was a conference.
Safety was the *ostensible* goal of the new rule.
Her *ostensible* neutrality fooled nobody.

senses.gloss: Done or made to impress people with how rich or important you are.
examples: The wedding was *ostentatious* — doves, fireworks, everything.
He drives an *ostentatious* gold car.
Her second house was *more ostentatious* than the first.

position: attributive only — *the other side*, never *this side is other*
contrast: *Another* is *an* + *other* and takes a singular noun: *another day*. *Others* is a pronoun: *Some stayed, others left*.

senses.gloss: The remaining one or ones of a group.
examples: The *other* shoe is under the bed.
All the *other* kids had already gone home.
I'll take this one; you take the *other* two.

senses.gloss: Different from the one already mentioned.
examples: Are there any *other* questions?
We should look at *other* options before signing.

contrast: An *-ly* word that is an adjective, not an adverb: *an otherworldly light*, never *she sang otherworldly*.

senses.gloss: Strange and beautiful in a way that does not seem to belong to this world.
examples: The desert at dawn looked *otherworldly*.
She sings in an *otherworldly* high voice.
The ice caves are *more otherworldly* than any photo shows.

form: from *Osman*, the founder of the dynasty
contrast: Lowercase *an ottoman* is a noun — a padded stool you rest your feet on.

senses.gloss: Of the Turkish empire that ruled from the 1300s to 1922.
examples: The city was under *Ottoman* rule for four centuries.
She studies *Ottoman* architecture in Istanbul.
The museum has a room of *Ottoman* tiles.

ru: отсутствующий; погасший; ставший известным; вышедший из моды
position: predicative only — *the lights are out*, never *the out lights*
contrast: *Out* is mostly an adverb (*go out*) and a preposition (*out the door*). Only after *be*, *go* or *come* is it an adjective.

senses.gloss: Not at home, not at work, not in the room.
examples: She's *out* until three if you want to call back.
Two of the drivers are *out* sick today.

senses.gloss: No longer burning, shining or working.
examples: The fire was *out* by midnight.
All the lights on the block were *out*.

senses.gloss: Known to everyone; published.
examples: The secret is *out* — everybody knows.
Her new album is *out* on Friday.

senses.gloss: No longer fashionable, or no longer possible.
examples: Skinny jeans are *out* again, apparently.
Driving is *out* — the road is closed.

senses.gloss: Open about being gay, lesbian or bisexual.
examples: He's been *out* since college.
She was the first *out* player in the league.

position: attributive only — *an out-and-out lie*, never *the lie was out-and-out*

senses.gloss: Complete and undeniable, used to make a negative word stronger.
examples: That's an *out-and-out* lie and he knows it.
The show was an *out-and-out* disaster.
He's an *out-and-out* crook.

position: both — *an out-of-bounds pass*; *the ball went out of bounds*
contrast: Americans drop the hyphens after a verb: *the ball is out of bounds*. Keep them before a noun.

senses.gloss: Outside the lines of the playing area.
examples: The receiver stepped *out of bounds* at the twenty.
It was an *out-of-bounds* kick, so they got the ball back.

senses.gloss: Off limits; not allowed.
examples: The kitchen is *out of bounds* to guests.
Questions about her family were *out of bounds*.

contrast: In American office slang, *I'll be out of pocket Thursday* means 'unreachable', not 'paying myself'.

senses.gloss: Paid with your own money, not covered by insurance or an employer.
examples: Her *out-of-pocket* costs came to eight hundred dollars.
The plan has a yearly *out-of-pocket* maximum.
Keep receipts for any *out-of-pocket* expenses.

senses.gloss: Far from where people usually go; hard to find.
examples: We found an *out-of-the-way* diner off the highway.
She grew up in an *out-of-the-way* mountain town.
They met in an *out-of-the-way* bar so nobody would see them.

contrast: After a verb, Americans say *from out of town*: *Half the guests are from out of town*.

senses.gloss: Coming from or happening in another town or city.
examples: We put the *out-of-town* guests in the motel by the highway.
The show had two *out-of-town* previews before Broadway.
*Out-of-town* buyers pushed the prices up.

form: compound — *out* + *board*, the side of a boat

senses.gloss: Mounted on the outside of a boat, or on the outer part of a wing.
examples: The skiff has a small *outboard* motor.
He rebuilt the *outboard* engine over the winter.
Fuel is stored in the *outboard* tanks of each wing.

position: both — *the outbound train*; *all the traffic is outbound*

senses.gloss: Traveling away from a place, or being sent out.
examples: The *outbound* train leaves from track 9.
*Outbound* flights were delayed by the storm.
The company blocks *outbound* email with attachments this big.

senses.gloss: No longer correct, useful or in use, because something newer exists.
examples: The website still runs on *outdated* software.
His ideas about parenting are badly *outdated*.
That map is *more outdated* than the one in the car.

ru: любящий природу, активный на свежем воздухе
position: both — mostly after a verb: *she's very outdoorsy*
contrast: Informal, and about people or their habits, not about places: say *an outdoor concert*, not *an outdoorsy concert*.

senses.gloss: Liking to spend time outside, hiking, camping and the like.
examples: I'm not *outdoorsy* — a hotel with a pool is my idea of nature.
They're an *outdoorsy* family; every vacation is a hike.
He got *more outdoorsy* after he bought the dog.

senses.gloss: Farthest from the center or the inside.
examples: Neptune is the *outermost* planet in the solar system.
Peel off the *outermost* layer of leaves.
They live on the *outermost* island in the chain.

senses.gloss: Friendly and comfortable meeting new people.
examples: He's the *outgoing* one; his brother barely talks.
You have to be *outgoing* to work the front desk.
She got *more outgoing* after a year in the dorms.

senses.gloss: Leaving a job or an official position.
examples: The *outgoing* governor gave a short farewell speech.
The *outgoing* board approved the budget on its last day.

senses.gloss: Being sent or going away from a place.
examples: Put the *outgoing* mail in the tray by the door.
All *outgoing* calls are recorded.

senses.gloss: So strange or extreme that it is hard to take seriously.
examples: He made an *outlandish* claim about aliens in the basement.
Her hats are *outlandish*, and she knows it.
Each excuse was *more outlandish* than the last.

senses.gloss: Far from the center of a town or region.
examples: Power is still out in the *outlying* neighborhoods.
The clinic serves three *outlying* villages.
Snow closed the roads to the *outlying* farms.

contrast: *Outmoded* suggests something has gone out of fashion; *outdated* is the everyday word for anything simply too old to be right.

senses.gloss: No longer used or accepted, because it belongs to an earlier time.
examples: The factory runs on *outmoded* equipment.
His views on women in the office are *outmoded*.
That teaching method is even *more outmoded* than the textbook.

contrast: The person is *outraged*; the thing that caused it is *outrageous*. *The outraged customers* left an *outrageous* review.

senses.gloss: Very angry because something seems deeply unfair or shocking.
examples: Parents were *outraged* by the school's decision.
*Outraged* callers jammed the station's phone lines.
She was *outraged* that no one had been told.

contrast: Don't mix it up with *outraged*: things are *outrageous*, people are *outraged*.

senses.gloss: Shocking and unacceptable.
examples: The fees they charge are *outrageous*.
It's *outrageous* that nobody was fired.
His behavior at the meeting was *more outrageous* than usual.

senses.gloss: Wildly unusual in a way that amuses or impresses people.
examples: She wore an *outrageous* pink wig to the party.
The comedian tells *outrageous* stories about his family.

position: attributive only — *the outside wall*, never *the wall is outside*
contrast: *Outside* is also a noun (*painted on the outside*), a preposition (*outside the house*) and an adverb (*let's eat outside*). Only the use before a noun is the adjective.

senses.gloss: On or facing the outer side.
examples: The *outside* walls need paint.
Take the *outside* lane for the exit.

senses.gloss: Coming from other people, not from inside the group.
examples: The company hired an *outside* consultant.
He has no *outside* interests besides fishing.

senses.gloss: Very small, about a chance.
examples: They still have an *outside* chance of making the playoffs.
There's an *outside* possibility that the flight is on time.

contrast: *Outsize* without the *-d* is a less common variant: *outsize clothing*.

senses.gloss: Much bigger than normal or than seems right.
examples: A few states have an *outsized* influence on the election.
He wore an *outsized* coat that reached his ankles.
The team's *outsized* payroll drew a lot of criticism.

position: both — *an outspoken critic*; *she has always been outspoken*

senses.gloss: Saying openly what you think, even when it may upset people.
examples: She's an *outspoken* critic of the new law.
He was *outspoken* about conditions at the plant.
The coach grew *more outspoken* after the third loss.

position: both — *an outstanding student*; *the balance is still outstanding*
contrast: The 'unpaid' sense is not gradable and sits mostly after a verb: *two bills are still outstanding*.

senses.gloss: Much better than the rest; excellent.
examples: She was an *outstanding* student in every subject.
The food was good; the service was *outstanding*.
His second novel is *more outstanding* than anything else on the list.

senses.gloss: Still not paid, finished or answered.
examples: There's an *outstanding* balance of $240 on the account.
Two questions from last week are still *outstanding*.

senses.gloss: Stretched out straight, about arms, hands or wings.
examples: She ran to him with *outstretched* arms.
The hawk glided by on *outstretched* wings.
He took the keys from my *outstretched* hand.

contrast: The adverb is *outward* or *outwards*: *the door opens outward*. Only the use before a noun is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Showing on the surface, whatever is really going on inside.
examples: His *outward* calm hid a lot of panic.
There was no *outward* sign that anything was wrong.

senses.gloss: Going away from a place or from the center.
examples: The *outward* journey took nine hours.
The blast caused an *outward* push in every direction.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the ovaries.
examples: The walk raises money for *ovarian* cancer research.
An *ovarian* cyst showed up on the scan.
The drug affects *ovarian* function.

position: predicative only — *the game is over*, never *the over game*
contrast: *Over* is usually a preposition (*over the bridge*) or an adverb (*come over*). Informally *I'm so over it* means 'I've stopped caring about it'.

senses.gloss: Finished; at an end.
examples: The game was *over* by nine.
Their marriage has been *over* for years.
Let's get the hard part *over* with first.

position: both — *an over-the-counter drug*; *the pills are over the counter now*
contrast: Often shortened to *OTC*. Americans drop the hyphens after a verb: *it's sold over the counter*.

senses.gloss: Sold without a doctor's prescription.
examples: Take an *over-the-counter* painkiller and rest.
The allergy pills went *over-the-counter* last year.
She keeps a shelf of *over-the-counter* medicine in the closet.

position: both — *an over-the-hill quarterback*; *he's over the hill*
contrast: Informal and rude if said to someone's face. After a verb the hyphens usually go: *at forty he was already over the hill*.

senses.gloss: Too old to do something as well as before.
examples: The team signed an *over-the-hill* quarterback for one season.
Forty is not *over the hill*, whatever the ads say.
His *over-the-hill* jokes got old fast.

position: both — *an over-the-top performance*; *the decorations were over the top*
contrast: Written without hyphens after a verb: *the whole thing was over the top*.

senses.gloss: Far too much; exaggerated past the point of good taste.
examples: His *over-the-top* performance ruined the scene for me.
The Halloween decorations are completely *over the top* this year.
Her apology was *more over-the-top* than the mistake.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an overactive imagination*

senses.gloss: Working or moving more than is normal or healthy.
examples: The tests showed an *overactive* thyroid.
There was no monster — just an *overactive* imagination.
Her immune system is *overactive* and attacks the joints.

contrast: *Overall* is also a common adverb: *Overall, the trip went well*. The noun *overalls* means a work garment — комбинезон.

senses.gloss: Counting everything together, not just one part.
examples: The *overall* cost came to nine thousand dollars.
Her *overall* health is good.
The *overall* winner gets a trip to Denver.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *that look is passe*
form: from French; usually printed with the accent, *passé*
contrast: A little bookish, and always about fashions and tastes, not about machines: say *an outdated printer*, not *a passe printer*.

senses.gloss: No longer fashionable.
examples: Fondue parties were *passe* by 1980.
He thinks neckties are *passe*.
Nothing looks *more passe* than last year's slang.

position: both — *a risque joke*; *the show was pretty risque*
form: from French; usually printed with the accent, *risqué*
contrast: A false friend for Russian speakers: *risque* is about sex and decency, not about danger. Risky business is *risky*.

senses.gloss: Slightly shocking because it deals with sex.
examples: He told a *risque* joke at the wedding and his wife glared.
The play was *risque* for 1955.
Her act got *more risque* as the night went on.

form: compound — *slap* + *stick*, the paddle clowns hit each other with
contrast: *Slapstick* is much more often a noun: *the movie is pure slapstick*. As an adjective it goes before words like *comedy*, *humor* and *routine*.

senses.gloss: Funny in a physical way — falling down, pies in the face, running into doors.
examples: The kids love the *slapstick* humor in those old shorts.
It's a *slapstick* comedy with three chase scenes.
He does a *slapstick* routine with a ladder and a bucket.

contrast: *Volunteer* is also a noun (*we need ten volunteers*) and a verb (*she volunteered to drive*). The adjective means 'unpaid, done by volunteers'.

senses.gloss: Done by people who help without being paid.
examples: She does *volunteer* work at the animal shelter.
Our town has a *volunteer* fire department.
The job is *volunteer*, but they cover your gas.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a well-behaved class*; open after a verb: *the kids were well behaved*
contrast: Comparison uses *better* and *best*, not *weller*: *the dog is better behaved than the cat*.

senses.gloss: Acting politely and doing what you are told, usually about children or animals.
examples: The kids were surprisingly *well behaved* at dinner.
She runs a *well-behaved* third-grade class.
Our dog is *better behaved* than the puppy next door.
